The spawning behaviour of Myctophum punctatum is intimately linked to the thermal regime of its mesopelagic habitat. During the reproductive period, which occurs under the stable thermal conditions of about 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C] in the North Atlantic, females release multiple batches of pelagic eggs. The maximum reproductive output is conveyed through two key metrics: each gravid female can produce roughly two eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly two eggs per spawning event], and these events can occur on a daily basis [F_R_i = events can occur on a daily basis], reflecting a high-frequency serial spawning strategy typical of small lanternfishes. This iteroparous mode, combined with the minuscule wet weight at birth of 0.000014 grams [Wwb = 0.000014 grams] for each newly hatched yolk-sac larva, underscores a life-history pattern geared toward high fecundity to offset the immense mortality pressures of the open ocean. The lecithotrophic prolarvae, after eclosion from the transparent, embryonated eggs, rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding.

As the endotrophic larvae deplete their yolk reserves and commence feeding, the growing juveniles undergo a period of rapid somatic expansion before reaching the critical developmental milestone of sexual maturation. The standard length at which individuals typically attain puberty is approximately 5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a fundamental shift in energy allocation from somatic growth toward reproductive investment. A fish reaching this length will have a corresponding wet weight at puberty of about 1.13 grams [Wwp = about 1.13 grams], as determined from length-weight regressions for the species. This transition from the actively feeding, pre-metamorphic larval stage to the post-metamorphic juvenile phase involves significant morphological transformation, including the ossification of fin rays and the development of the characteristic photophore patterns. The attainment of this pubertal length is generally recorded within the first year of life, although the exact timing is modulated by local food availability and the ambient temperature of the water column.

The ultimate maximum size a Spotted lanternfish can achieve as a sexually mature adult, representing its asymptotic body length, is 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters]. This definitive standard length is rarely attained in the wild, as most individuals are subject to predation or energetic constraints before reaching this maximum. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for an individual of this length is estimated to be 13.5 grams [Wwi = 13.5 grams], a value derived from morphometric relationships established in the laboratory. This mass, while modest compared to epipelagic fishes, is substantial for a mesopelagic migrator that must efficiently navigate the energetic costs of daily vertical migrations. Comparative analyses with other myctophids, such as the larger Notoscopelus elongatus, indicate that the asymptotic size of M. punctatum is characteristic of species occupying a mid-trophic position within the oceanic food web, where body size is a key determinant of gape-limited predation and metabolic efficiency.

The longevity of Myctophum punctatum under natural, thermally stable conditions in its deep-water environment is impressive for such a small teleost. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species, observed in individuals maintained at a consistent temperature of 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C], is 35,770 days [am = 35,770 days]. This remarkably extended life span, more characteristic of deep-sea or cold-water organisms, is a direct consequence of the slowed metabolic rates and reduced predation pressure at depth. Such an extended life history contrasts sharply with the brief, often semelparous lives of many epipelagic forage fishes and suggests a strategy of slow but sustained reproductive output over many decades. Indeed, a sexually mature individual that first spawned at 5 centimeters in length can continue to reproduce for the vast majority of its long life, releasing eggs daily during each spawning season.

An important consequence of this slow metabolic pace is the modulation of the maximum daily reproduction rate. When the ambient water temperature is 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C], the species achieves its highest recorded spawning frequency of one event per day [F_R_i = one event per day] coupled with a modest clutch size of approximately two eggs [N_R_i = clutch size of approximately two eggs]. This yields a daily reproductive rate of roughly 2 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 2 eggs per day], a value that represents the peak fecundity under optimal thermal conditions. A broader ecological perspective reveals that the lanternfish's life-history syndrome—combining a tiny birth weight, a late onset of reproduction at 5 centimeters, a long reproductive window, and an extraordinary lifespan—is finely tuned to the stable, resource-poor environment of the mesopelagic zone. The ability to reproduce frequently over a period of decades ensures that even a single individual can contribute significantly to the next generation, buffering the population against the stochastic recruitment failures that plague many short-lived marine species.
